journal.intro: Short reads on the practice: what happens on the board, and how to keep coming back.

guide.title: How to stand on the board
guide.lead: A short ritual. The board does the work; your part is to stay and breathe.

p: Put the board on a flat surface that doesn't slip. A rug or a yoga mat keeps it in place.
Stand barefoot, with a table, a wall or a friend's hands within reach.
Never stand with wounds or skin infections on your feet. If you have a health condition, read the safety answer in Questions first.
Step on with one foot, then slowly shift your weight and bring the other. Holding on is fine.
Keep your knees soft, not locked, and let your weight spread evenly across both feet.
Rest your gaze on one point in front of you. Breathe at your own pace; just don't hold your breath.
The first seconds are the sharpest. The sensation peaks, then eases into warmth. Riding that wave is the practice.
Start with 30 to 60 seconds. Listen to yourself and build up to two minutes and beyond.
Hold on and step off one foot at a time. Stay on the floor for a moment and notice the warmth and tingling.
Small red dots on your soles are normal and fade within an hour.

faq.title: Questions
faq.lead: Short answers to what people ask most.

p: Yes, at first. The sharpest part is the first 10 to 30 seconds; then it usually turns into warmth and tingling. If the pain becomes stabbing or doesn't ease, step off.
Start with 30 to 60 seconds. Many people settle at 2 to 5 minutes, some go to 10 or more. The 21-day program on Home raises the time gradually.
A little every day works better than long, rare sessions. Once a day is plenty.
Mornings wake you up, evenings help you unwind. Pick the time you can keep, and set a reminder in Settings.

Talk to a doctor first if you are pregnant, have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet, varicose veins or thrombosis, a bleeding disorder or take blood thinners, epilepsy, a heart condition, or a recent foot injury or surgery.
Never stand with open wounds or skin infections on your feet.
No. Gvozdi is a practice companion, not medical advice. It doesn't diagnose or treat anything.

sections.h: What are the dots on my feet?
p: Small red marks are normal pressure marks and fade within an hour or so. Bruises or broken skin mean the session was too long for now: rest a day and go shorter next time.

sections.h: Which nail spacing should I choose?
p: The wider the spacing, the fewer nails share your weight, and the stronger it feels. Tighter spacing is gentler and a good place to start.

about.title: About gvozdi
about.lead: A calm companion for nail-board practice.

p: The app keeps time while you stand, so you can close your eyes and let the wave pass.
It grew out of StepSure, our earlier app, and is made by a small independent team.
We keep only what the app needs: your sessions, notes and settings. Usage analytics help us improve the app, and you can switch them off in Settings. We never sell your data.
Questions, ideas or a bug? Write to us on Telegram. And please, take care of yourself.

first-minutes.title: The first two minutes
first-minutes.lead: Why the hardest part comes first, and what to do with it.

p: Every session has the same shape. You step on, and within seconds the sensation climbs to a sharp peak. Everything in you says: get off. This is where most people quit.
If you stay, something shifts. Somewhere between thirty seconds and a minute, the sharpness turns into heat, then into a wide, humming warmth. The peak passed while you were busy enduring it.
That's why a Peak session shows a curve: to remind you that the wave will crest and fall. You don't have to like the peak. You only have to let it pass.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Soften your knees and your jaw. Count breaths, not seconds.
There is nothing to win. Two calm minutes are worth more than ten clenched ones.

why-feet.title: Why the feet
why-feet.lead: A lot of you lives in your soles.

p: Your soles are among the most sensitive skin you have, packed with nerve endings that tell you about every pebble. That's why a board of blunt nails takes all of your attention so quickly.
Strong, safe sensation pulls you into the present. It's hard to rehearse tomorrow's meeting while your feet are this loud. People often call it meditation for those who can't sit still.

You'll find bold promises online. We'd rather be honest: research on nail boards is thin. What people do report, again and again, is a clear head, warm feet and the quiet pride of doing something hard on purpose. That's enough for us.

habit.title: Small and daily
habit.lead: How to make standing a habit that stays.

p: Habits grow from repetition, not intensity. Two minutes every day will change more than half an hour once a week.
Stand right after brushing your teeth, or while the kettle boils. A routine you already have is the best reminder.
Out of sight, out of practice. Leave the board where you'll see it every morning.
Life happens. Your streak starts over, but your progress stays: the 21-day program simply pauses and waits for you.
The reminder, the streak and the tree are there to help you, never to judge you.

after.title: After you step off
after.lead: The minute after the board is part of the practice.

p: Don't rush away. Stand on the floor with your eyes closed and feel your feet. Most people notice heat, tingling and a sense of weight sinking into the ground.
It's a good moment to notice how you feel and write a line in the session note. Over weeks, these notes show patterns that a timer can't.
Walk barefoot for a minute. Have a glass of water if you like. If your soles feel tender the next day, rest; the board will wait.
